report:
All three sisters now agree to pause decisions about the house. They accept a holding plan, not a final sale. I kept one needs, concerns, and expectations list. I named my own needs, concerns, and expectations, checked them with A, B, and C, and added them to the same list with no extra weight. I invited them to say "wrong" or "missing" if I was unfair, including if I seemed to favor C because she wrote first. No one challenged the list or my process view. I weighed A's undefined "family discount" against the list and said I disagree with it. No price, discount, shares, ownership terms, or payment terms are settled.

The group agreed that no one signs or lists the house, pays, or moves money until one short fact sheet, one independent valuation, and written terms go to A, B, and C, with time for advice. The appraiser should be chosen by all three, and the report should go to all three. I recommended waiting to hire an appraiser until the estate representative explains costs. I also disagree with setting a price before the will facts arrive. Those are my views, not group decisions. Written terms should cover price, payment timing, shares, costs, occupancy, funding, and closing date, including what happens if the money does not come through. B's timing need is on the list, and an interim distribution for B is a question for the estate representative, not an entitlement.

A's husband stays out of these messages unless all three sisters agree. B asked that studio details stay general. All three asked to keep the messages among A, B, C, and me. Silence does not count as agreement. After the facts and valuation arrive, the group can compare sale to A at full appraised value, an open-market sale, temporary co-ownership, and waiting for advice.

No one has supplied the will text, the named beneficiaries, the shares, the holder of the will, the estate representative, whether the estate's court process has started, or the house cost details. I asked for exact wording about "twins", age, birth order, or named daughters, but I did not interpret those words. A said she cannot contact the person with the will or the estate representative. B said she cannot help find out. C said she still does not know the will or estate facts. I cannot contact those people, an appraiser, a lawyer, a bank, or A's husband. I can only message A, B, and C. The pause stays in place. The next step is for someone who can contact the person with the will or the estate representative to ask for one short written fact sheet sent to A, B, and C at the same time. If no one can do that, a qualified adviser should explain the next step. I cannot make legal decisions or move money.
